items.reason: 'north of the Line' uses the sailor's term for the equator, unexplained in this chapter; a first-time reader or listener may not know it. Brief accurate gloss added.
items.new: "Some two years before I first learned of the events I am about to recount to you, gentlemen, the Town-Ho, Sperm Whaler of Nantucket, was cruising in your Pacific here, not very many days' sail eastward from the eaves of this good Golden Inn. She was somewhere to the north of the Line (the equator). One morning, when the pumps were worked, as was the daily custom, it was noticed that she was taking more water into her hold than usual. They supposed a swordfish had stabbed her, gentlemen. But the captain had some unusual reason for believing that rare good luck awaited him in those latitudes, and was therefore very unwilling to leave them; and since the leak was not then considered at all dangerous (though, in fact, they could not find it after searching the hold as low down as was possible in rather heavy weather), the ship went on with her cruising, the sailors working at the pumps at long and easy intervals. But no good luck came. More days went by, and not only was the leak still undiscovered, but it noticeably increased. So much so that the captain, now taking some alarm, made all sail and headed for the nearest harbor among the islands, to have his hull hove out and repaired there."

items.reason: 'planted their group of hands on it' is an odd phrase that stops the reader; 'all planted their hands on it' keeps the image (several men pressing down the slide).
items.new: "As the Lakeman's bare head was just level with the planks, the Captain and his posse leaped the barricade, and, rapidly drawing the slide of the scuttle over, all planted their hands on it and loudly called for the steward to bring the heavy brass padlock belonging to the companionway. Then, opening the slide a little, the Captain whispered something down the crack, closed it, and turned the key on them — ten in number — leaving on deck some twenty or more, who so far had remained neutral."

items.reason: Final sentence parses as 'all hands were turned to, and sullenly worked by the moody seamen' until the reader reaches 'the iron pumps'; a comma after 'and' marks the participle phrase as belonging to the pumps.
items.new: "'So I am, but take that.' The mate was in the very act of striking when another hiss stayed his raised arm. He paused — and then pausing no more, made good on his word, in spite of Steelkilt's threat, whatever that might have been. The three men were then cut down, all hands were turned to, and, sullenly worked by the moody seamen, the iron pumps clanged as before."

items.reason: 'trick at the helm' (nautical: a spell or turn of duty steering) is used here and again in 54.77 without explanation; a reader may take 'trick' as a ruse, which is a real risk in a revenge plot. Brief gloss on first use.
items.new: "During the night, Radney had an unseamanlike way of sitting on the bulwarks of the quarter-deck and leaning his arm on the gunwale of the boat that was hoisted up there, a little above the ship's side. In this position, it was well known, he sometimes dozed. There was a considerable gap between the boat and the ship, and down through it lay the sea. Steelkilt calculated his time, and found that his next trick (his turn of duty) at the helm would come round at two o'clock in the morning of the third day from the one on which he had been betrayed. At his leisure, he spent the interval braiding something very carefully during his watches below."

items.reason: 'Twenty-four hours later, his trick at the silent helm — ... — that fatal hour was then to come' has a dangling subject that the reader must reread to connect to 'that fatal hour'. Reordered so the sentence parses, keeping every element.
items.new: "'Why not? Do you think he won't do me a turn, when it's to help himself in the end, shipmate?' And going to the mate, he looked at him quietly and asked him for some twine to mend his hammock. It was given him — neither twine nor lanyard was ever seen again; but the next night an iron ball, closely netted, partly rolled out of the pocket of the Lakeman's monkey jacket as he was tucking the coat into his hammock for a pillow. Twenty-four hours later would come his trick at the silent helm — close beside the man who was apt to doze over the grave always dug ready to the seaman's hand — and that fatal hour was then to come; and in the foreordaining soul of Steelkilt, the mate already lay stark and stretched out as a corpse, with his forehead crushed in."
